# Architecture Data, Knowledge, and Representation {#sec-data-representations-world-models}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world."*
>
> — Ludwig Wittgenstein, *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* (1922) [@Wittgenstein1922Tractatus]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Ludwig Wittgenstein tied the limits of language to the limits
of one's world. The architecture claim is narrower. A method can change only
the design state exposed to it. If a representation has no way to express a
coherence assumption, software dependency, or physical limit, the method
cannot preserve it deliberately.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What must an AI-assisted architecture system preserve when its data comes from
changing designs, costly tools, workloads, and sources that do not always
agree?
:::

An image-classification dataset can present each item as an array of pixels and
a label. An architecture result cannot be reduced to a number and a name. A
cycle count, timing report, or power estimate applies to a particular design,
software image, workload, tool path, version, and set of conditions. One wrong
connection or protocol assumption can invalidate the design even when its text
looks similar to many valid examples.

Architecture data also arrives in forms that were created for different jobs.
Specifications state requirements. Source code and register-transfer-level
(RTL) designs define executable or buildable artifacts. Traces record selected
workload behavior. Simulators, formal tools, synthesis flows, physical-design
tools, prototypes, and silicon return different measurements and check results.
Review comments and rejected alternatives preserve decisions that no tool
report contains. These sources differ in access, freshness, cost, coverage, and
what they can establish.

A *representation* is the form in which selected properties of a source or
design are made available to a method. A native RTL file, a typed graph, a table
of measurements, a retrieval index, and a learned embedding can all represent
part of an architecture problem. None preserves everything. The choice
determines which relationships remain visible, which designs can be expressed,
and which mistakes a later method may fail to notice.

Raw sources become useful data only after the project identifies them, aligns
their versions and units, records the conditions under which they were
obtained, and checks that their labels or tool returns mean what the dataset
claims. Some of that data becomes durable project knowledge. Other parts remain
live project state that must change with the checked-in design, software,
workload, constraints, and unresolved issues. An architecture foundation model
may supply broad prior knowledge about mechanisms and common designs. Its
weights do not contain the authoritative truth about the current project.

This chapter explains how to construct that information without collapsing it
into one dataset or one learned vector. It ends with a linked account of native
artifacts, checked data, project knowledge, explicit state, and learned
representations that @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization can use to
choose an approach. It does not select that method, design the tool environment,
or decide whether a returned measurement supports a design conclusion.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Distinguish architecture data from interchangeable labeled examples and name
  the source conditions that give each sample meaning.
- Connect workloads, tool results, cost, missingness, and coverage to the
  design and software state that produced them.
- Build and check a dataset without confusing invalid requests, tool failures,
  measured violations, unknown outcomes, and successful samples.
- Separate recorded data, durable project knowledge, and live project state,
  and identify the responsible source for each current fact.
- Connect native artifacts to structured and learned representations while
  preserving identity, legality, units, constraints, uncertainty, and check
  results.
- Hand a later method an inspectable architecture problem without prescribing
  generation, prediction, or optimization.

:::

## Why Architecture Data Is Different

Architecture data is heterogeneous, conditional, expensive to acquire, and
often proprietary. A specification paragraph, an RTL module, a performance
counter trace, and a routed timing report are not interchangeable samples. Each
preserves different relationships and omits different conditions. Their
differences are part of the data rather than noise to remove.

Rows also share dependencies. Two results may come from the same design
ancestor, generated artifact, workload trace, software image, tool model, or
earlier decision. A failed physical-design run may return no complete metric,
while a timing check may establish only that a threshold was crossed. Counting
these records as independent examples with fixed labels would hide both their
lineage and their missingness.

Architecture correctness adds a harder boundary. A plausible token sequence can
still connect the wrong signals, violate a protocol, drop a reset condition, or
refer to a stale hierarchy. More superficially similar examples do not repair
the omitted relationship. A usable representation must therefore preserve the
structure and conditions that let a tool or reviewer detect the mistake.

The sources may remain in separate project systems. A configuration schema,
workload manifest, repository revision, run directory, and review record do not
need to become one database. They do need shared identities that let another
architect determine which artifacts and measurements describe the same design
and conditions. That requirement leads first to the sources from which
architecture data is built.

## Sources of Architecture Data

Papers, specifications, source code, RTL, traces, tool reports, failed
candidates, review notes, and field observations preserve different
relationships. The relevant distinction is not text versus numbers. It is
which question a source can answer, which context it omits, and how a reader
can connect it to the current design (@tbl-dataset-capability).

| **Source Structure** | **What It Can Preserve** | **What It Cannot Establish Alone** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paper, manual, or specification | Concepts, requirements, interfaces, prior findings, and source-linked rationale. | The current project version or whether a local implementation satisfies the requirement. |
| Question and answer or design note | Focused reasoning, calculations, and review rationale. | Executable state, complete dependencies, or conditions not written into the note. |
| Code, RTL, configuration, or typed intermediate representation | Concrete structure, parameter values, interfaces, and buildable state within the properties the format expresses. | Workload coverage, design intent, or physical effects that require later tools. |
| Workload trace or profile | Observed software behavior under a stated capture or sampling policy. | Behavior outside the captured population or effects the collection method cannot observe. |
| Tool run and report | A result under a particular design, tool, configuration, seed, model, and workload. | A general rule beyond those conditions. |
| Rejected candidate or review decision | A boundary that mattered, the conditions that exposed it, and the reason work stopped. | Whether the same rejection still applies after the design or conditions change. |

: **Source structure determines what can be carried into later work.** More
data does not repair a missing relationship, version, or condition.
{#tbl-dataset-capability tbl-colwidths="[24,36,30]"}

Read each row from the source structure to the relationships it preserves and
then to the claim it cannot establish alone. Code or RTL can describe buildable
structure but not workload coverage or later physical effects. A tool report
binds a result to conditions but does not establish a general rule, and a
rejected candidate preserves a boundary only while its recorded conditions
still apply. More source volume cannot make one structure authoritative for
fields it does not own.

The responsible source may also be private, licensed, or access-restricted.
That boundary does not make a convenient public substitute authoritative. The
representation should retain the source identity, version, responsible owner,
access limit, and conditions under which it applies, with a link that an
authorized reviewer can resolve.

Field and fleet observations need further acquisition context. Record the
deployed hardware and software versions, workload population, sampling policy,
measurement conditions, privacy or redaction rules, and collection cost with
the observation. A result from deployed systems describes that version and
population. It does not automatically become a training label or a conclusion
about the next design.

This is one reason architecture data differs from a conventional image
classification dataset. A label such as *cat* can be useful without a build
manifest. A cycle count, power estimate, or timing failure is uninterpretable
without the design, workload, tool path, and assumptions that produced it.
Hardware also has hard structural boundaries. One wrong connection can make a
design unusable, and tightly coupled changes can move performance, power,
timing, area, and software behavior together. A large corpus of disconnected
artifacts does not recover those relationships.

Public availability is only the first filter. The OpenRTLSet collection started
with approximately 103,000 permissively licensed public C/C++ repositories.
The authors' synthesizability screen retained approximately 12,000, and their
Vitis HLS flow successfully generated Verilog from approximately 1,000
repositories [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. @fig-public-code-to-rtl shows these
three stages with the same unit, repositories. The resulting 24,000 Verilog
modules are shown as an annotation because one successful repository can
produce many modules, so module count is not a fourth attrition stage.

```{python}
#| label: fig-public-code-to-rtl
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Public code becomes architecture data only after several filters.** In the OpenRTLSet C/C++ collection path, approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories became approximately 12,000 repositories after the authors' synthesizability screen, and approximately 1,000 successfully produced Verilog through their Vitis HLS flow [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. The reported 24,000 output modules use a different unit and therefore appear as an annotation rather than another point. These pipeline-specific counts are not universal GitHub or HLS success rates.
#| out-width: "88%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale connected-dot plot with three stages from the OpenRTLSet C and C++ collection pipeline. Approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories enter the pipeline, 12,000 remain after the authors' synthesizability screen, and 1,000 successfully generate Verilog through Vitis HLS. A separate note states that the successful repositories produced approximately 24,000 Verilog modules, which is a different unit."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Values are approximate counts transcribed from Sections III-A1 and III-A2 of
# OpenRTLSet [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. Receipt:
# data/source-receipts/chapter4-openrtlset-funnel.csv. Accessed 2026-07-30.
stages = [
    "Permissively licensed\nC/C++ repositories",
    "After authors'\nsynthesizability screen",
    "Successful Vitis HLS\nto Verilog",
]
counts = [103_000, 12_000, 1_000]
display_counts = ["≈103,000", "≈12,000", "≈1,000"]
y = [2, 1, 0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.7, 2.55))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.38, right=0.92, top=0.88, bottom=0.30)

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(500, 220_000)
ax.plot(counts, y, color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=1.2, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(
    counts,
    y,
    s=46,
    color=COLORS["workload"],
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=0.8,
    zorder=2,
)

for x_value, y_value, label in zip(counts, y, display_counts):
    ax.text(
        x_value * 1.14,
        y_value,
        label,
        ha="left",
        va="center",
        fontsize=6.4,
        fontweight="bold",
        color=COLORS["workload_ink"],
    )

ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(stages, fontsize=6.2)
ax.set_xlabel("approximate repositories remaining (log scale)", fontsize=6.2)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.0, length=2.5, width=0.6)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, pad=5)
ax.grid(axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)
ax.text(
    0.0,
    -0.36,
    "Output annotation: ≈24,000 Verilog modules from ≈1,000 successful repositories",
    transform=ax.transAxes,
    ha="left",
    va="top",
    fontsize=5.8,
    color=COLORS["muted"],
)

for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

Read from top to bottom. About 11.7 percent of the starting repositories
survived the authors' initial screen, and about 1 percent successfully produced
Verilog through this particular pipeline. Those derived ratios describe the
authors' repository search, license policy, screen, and tool flow. They do not
estimate how much public C/C++ is synthesizable in general. The example makes a
narrower point. Collecting public source, deciding what is legally usable,
screening it, executing a conversion tool, and retaining failures are distinct
dataset-engineering steps.

Two other public datasets make the source difference concrete. RTL-Repo keeps full
repository context around more than 4,000 public Verilog samples
[@AllamShalan2024RTLRepo]. CircuitNet records graph and image representations
from a declared synthesis and physical-design flow
[@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet]. It attempted 12,960 back-end runs and retained
10,242 layouts after excluding failed runs [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet]. These
datasets support different questions. Neither supplies the current state or
complete history of a live design project. CircuitNet's retained layouts also
illustrate a general dataset risk. A model trained only on the surviving
layouts can learn the properties of completed runs without learning where the
flow failed or why.

QuArch provides another public source with a different purpose. Its
question-answer dataset tests access to knowledge about architecture concepts
and prior designs [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch]. It does not identify a current
project revision, software image, workload, constraints, or responsible source,
so it cannot supply live project state.

Public sources make comparison and reuse possible, but they usually omit
proprietary design context. Community datasets can preserve declared
repositories, flows, and collection choices, yet their quality depends on what
contributors record and release. Internal sources may carry the current design,
review history, and vendor material that a real decision needs, but privacy,
intellectual-property, license, and access limits constrain how they are used.
The dataset must preserve that access status rather than silently replacing a
restricted source with a convenient public one.

One source remains central to almost every architecture result. The workload
determines which parts of the hardware and software become active.

## Workloads as Data and Experimental Inputs {#sec-workload-phase-behavior}

Static hardware does not identify what it will run. A workload record must
carry the software image, inputs, scale, trace or profile, phase definitions,
sampling policy, runtime settings, and coverage limits relevant to the study.
Those fields are not background metadata. They determine which hardware
behavior becomes visible.

The Lighthouse XR workload is bursty and phase dependent. A trace can expose
frame boundaries, memory behavior, and periods of activity. It may still omit
timing feedback that would have changed the instruction stream, thread
interleaving, or system behavior. A trace captured under one software image
cannot silently stand in for another. The representation must connect
`XR-TRACE-A` to `SW-BASE-A`, its frame identifiers, its collection policy, and
the hardware conditions under which it is used.

Representative sampling can reduce detailed simulation cost without changing
the simulator itself. SimPoint clusters recurring execution phases and
simulates representative intervals, while SMARTS uses statistical sampling and
reports confidence for the estimate
[@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The durable
representation point is not which sampling scheme to choose. It is that the
selected intervals, weights, and coverage become part of workload state. A
sampled result without those fields cannot be interpreted or reproduced.

Representativeness is specific to the claim. A workload that exercises a cache
capacity decision may not exercise an accelerator interface, an operating
system transition, or the thermal behavior of a deployed workload mix. Every
measurement must therefore remain linked to the exact workload artifact and
design state that produced it. Once those conditions are explicit, the project
can ask what one such sample costs and what part of the design space it covers.

## Cost and Coverage of a Sample

The same design may be examined with an analytical model, trace replay,
cycle-level simulator, RTL simulation, formal analysis, FPGA platform, or
fabricated silicon.
These sources differ in cost, speed, abstraction, and observability
(@fig-observation-source-choice, @tbl-observation-source-limits). They do not form one
fidelity ranking for every property. Gate-level analysis may preserve target
timing detail that an FPGA mapping does not, while an FPGA platform may execute
far more workload than that analysis can cover. Silicon can reveal behavior of
the fabricated design but cannot recover a counterfactual configuration that
was never built.

![**Choose observation sources for the property and decision.** Analytical,
trace-driven, cycle-level, RTL or gate-level, FPGA or emulation, and silicon
sources offer different coverage, costs, conditions, and blind spots. A study
may combine them, and each recorded observation retains that
context.](images/F4-data-pyramid){#fig-observation-source-choice
fig-alt="A study starts with the architecture property it must observe, then
compares six observation sources shown without a universal ranking:
analytical models, trace-driven models, cycle-level simulation, RTL or
gate-level analysis, FPGA or emulation, and fabricated silicon. Each obtained
observation retains its source and version, property coverage, acquisition
cost, conditions, and blind spots." width="100%"}

The study starts with the property it must observe, then compares candidate
sources by coverage, cost, conditions, and blind spots. It may choose several.
The six sources appear in parallel because none is uniformly more informative
than the others. When a source produces an observation, its record keeps the
context needed to interpret and compare it. The choice follows the property and
decision rather than a generic fidelity rank.

The overview groups major observation paths rather than every distinct return
type. An observation becomes usable only when its appropriate use is paired
with the limit and provenance its representation must retain
(@tbl-observation-source-limits). The table separates simulation, formal
analysis, and implementation-facing flows because they return different kinds
of results.

| **Source** | **Useful For** | **Important Limit to Represent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical model | Fast sensitivity studies and early bounds. | Simplifying equations, calibration range, and omitted interactions. |
| Trace-driven model | Repeatable study of behavior contained in a captured instruction or event stream. | No behavior that depends on timing feedback absent from the trace. |
| Cycle-level simulator | Detailed modeled microarchitectural behavior. | Simulator abstractions, unsupported states, calibration, and execution cost. |
| RTL simulation | Logic, interface, and microarchitectural behavior over the exercised testbench and observed properties. | Stimulus and testbench identity, functional and code coverage, unknown-value handling, simulator version, and timing abstractions. |
| Formal analysis | Proof, counterexample, bounded-only, or inconclusive status for a stated property, model, and assumptions. | Exact property and assumptions, abstraction, proof method, bound or completeness argument, vacuity checks, and returned status. |
| Synthesis or gate-level implementation flow | Logic transformation and implementation-facing timing, area, power, or rule checks within the executed flow. | Libraries, modes, corners, constraints, waivers, tool versions, and physical effects outside the flow. |
| FPGA or emulation platform | High-throughput functional or timing-model execution after mapping. | Mapping differences, compile cost, debug visibility, and non-transferable ASIC power or timing. |
| Fabricated silicon | Behavior of a physical implementation under measured conditions. | Limited design variants, observability, stepping, test conditions, and inability to answer every counterfactual question. |

: **Every observation source has a useful scope and a blind spot.** The
representation records both so that later chapters can choose and evaluate a
tool path for the actual question.
{#tbl-observation-source-limits tbl-colwidths="[20,34,36]"}

Analytical and trace-driven sources provide fast or repeatable results but omit
interactions or timing feedback. RTL simulation observes exercised behavior,
formal analysis returns a scoped logical status, and synthesis or gate-level
flows add implementation assumptions and constraints. FPGA, emulation, and
silicon extend throughput or physical observation while retaining limits in
mapping, observability, and the ability to examine unbuilt alternatives. The
rows do not order the sources. The property under study determines which
limits are acceptable and whether several sources are needed.

These costs also shape the available data. Expensive observation paths usually
produce fewer observations, and only observations with compatible designs,
workloads, tools, and conditions can support a direct comparison. A large
collection of incompatible reports does not become a dense dataset for the
current study.

BOOM-Explorer makes the acquisition cost concrete. Each high-fidelity
VLSI-flow evaluation for its dataset of 994 legal microarchitectures took about
six hours at the low end and more than fourteen hours at the high end
[@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer].

A stored result also needs an acquisition record. It should
identify the kind and fidelity of the tool run, whether the run completed,
failed, timed out, or was retried, and the repeated seeds or configurations
that produced the result. When available, it should also retain uncertainty or
an interval reported by the source, execution and queue time, compute and memory
use, tool or license use, and the human work required for setup, diagnosis,
review, and repair. Ten analytical-model calls,
ten cycle-level simulations, and ten physical-design runs may each create ten
rows, but they do not represent the same cost, coverage, or opportunity to
observe failure. When an exact monetary cost is unavailable, the representation
should preserve the separate resource counts rather than omit them or collapse
them into one number.

Those resource counts belong in the representation even though later work will
use them to choose methods, manage tools, interpret measurements, and compare
complete systems. A stored result must name enough of its source conditions and
acquisition cost for an architect to decide whether it applies and what it took
to produce.

Taken together, the earlier cat-label contrast, the source-cost spectrum, and
the acquisition record show why architecture results are not interchangeable
examples with fixed labels. Architecture samples are costly, conditioned
results tied to a design history and a set of property checks
(@tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels).

| **Dataset simplification** | **Architecture sample** | **Consequence for later use** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cheap acquisition | A result may require scarce licenses, long tool runs, fabrication, setup, diagnosis, and expert review. | Record the resources and human work needed to obtain or fail to obtain it. |
| Fixed ground-truth label | A simulator, verifier, or physical tool returns a result for a named property at a stated fidelity and under recorded conditions. | Preserve the property, check, fidelity, and conditions for later interpretation. |
| Independent, interchangeable rows | Results may share a design ancestor, generated artifact, workload trace, software image, model, seed, or earlier decision. | Preserve lineage and do not count dependent results as independent support. |
| Missing data without structure | Failed, timed-out, and rejected runs are selectively lost, while some violations reveal only that a threshold was crossed. | Retain run status, failure reason, and censored bounds instead of learning only from survivors. |
| Same fields imply comparability | Two rows support a direct comparison only when their candidate identities and permitted differences are explicit and the workload, software, tool path, and relevant conditions match. | Keep results with uncontrolled differences as advisory context rather than treating them as samples from the same comparison. |

: **Architecture samples are costly, conditioned results.** Their meaning and
comparability depend on lineage, property checks, acquisition status, and
matched study conditions.
{#tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels tbl-colwidths="[23,42,35]"}

These distinctions change what a stored dataset row contains. A timing row does
not attach a universal correct or incorrect label to a cache. It preserves the
status returned by a named timing check together with the library, constraints,
corner, and tool state. A failed or absent result preserves its run status and
failure reason rather than silently becoming a poor design. Later
interpretation determines whether the return marks a feasibility boundary, an
infrastructure failure, or no usable measurement. The failed-run records in
@tbl-negative-traces keep those possibilities separate.

## Building and Checking a Usable Dataset

Collecting files does not create a dataset. Construction begins with the
architecture decision the data must support. The project then defines the unit
of observation, the designs and workloads that must be covered, the properties
to be measured, and the failures or unknown outcomes that must remain visible.
Those choices determine which sources are needed and which expensive tool calls
are worth acquiring.

Coverage needs an acquisition plan before a learned method or optimizer begins
choosing points. The plan declares the legal design regions, workloads,
conditions, and outcomes that the dataset must support. Its initial samples
should cover those groups without placing related designs or workload
derivatives on both sides of a later evaluation. When active learning or
multifidelity selection chooses subsequent runs, every observation retains the
selection rule, its version, the available candidate set, and the observations
available at the time [@Settles2009ActiveLearning;
@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. Adaptively acquired data
describes the region that the selection policy visited. It is not an unbiased
map of the legal design space.

The acquisition process must retain attempted points, failures, and censored
returns, and it must reserve design or workload groups that the selector cannot
consume. These requirements let a later reviewer distinguish broad support
from dense sampling near a predicted optimum. Method selection belongs to
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. The present chapter records
how that choice shaped the dataset.

For a tool-derived dataset, one row should identify a design, software image,
workload, tool and model version, conditions, and execution attempt before it
stores a metric. Specifications, RTL or compiler graphs, traces, and tool
reports can then be aligned through those identities. Cleaning checks units,
schemas, version consistency, duplicate lineage, stale artifacts, and whether
the recorded result came from the candidate named by the row. A normalized
number with the wrong parent design is still bad data.

The prospective Lighthouse cache comparison makes that construction sequence
concrete. Its decision is whether a 3 or 4\ MB L2 candidate should advance
against a rerun 2\ MB baseline. The unit of observation is not “a cache.” It
is one named capacity candidate evaluated with `XR-COMPUTE-A`,
`SW-BASE-A`, `XR-TRACE-A`, and the declared simulator, power, SRAM, and
process assumptions. The required coverage includes the workload frames and
tail-latency behavior used by the decision, all three capacity choices, and
the physical limits that can reject a candidate.

The acquisition plan has a fixed budget: one SRAM evaluation per capacity and
four cycle-level executions including infrastructure reruns. A retry consumes
budget but does not create a new independent candidate sample. Each attempt
therefore keeps its own status and logs, while completed measurements join the
candidate and condition identities that make a comparison valid. The limited
budget favors measurements that can distinguish the two larger candidates
from the rerun baseline; it does not justify filling an unmeasured condition
with a model estimate and labeling it as observed.

The split must follow the transfer claim. If the dataset is used to test
transfer to the current XR subsystem, rows derived from `XR-COMPUTE-A` or
`XR-TRACE-A` cannot be scattered between training and evaluation. The current
design, workload, or a later time period must remain held out as a group. If
no different designs or workloads exist for training, the dataset does not
support a transfer claim. It still supports the narrower, within-study
capacity comparison. This walkthrough ends with an explicit limitation: even
a complete cache table says nothing by itself about another cache policy,
software path, workload population, or physical implementation.

Outcome categories must survive this alignment. An invalid request, dependency
failure, infrastructure failure, incomplete run, measured limit violation,
formal result, and unknown outcome answer different questions. Collapsing them
into a binary success label teaches a later method that a broken license server
and a physically infeasible candidate mean the same thing.

Public benchmarks add another risk. Models trained on public HDL corpora may
have seen the standard benchmark solutions, and contamination studies have
found this pattern in common Verilog benchmarks [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated].
The same concern appears in broader language-model evaluation
[@Balloccu2024Leakage]. A benchmark score cannot establish general design
ability when the evaluated artifacts may have appeared in training. Held-out
designs, source identity, and executable checks matter more than the volume of
examples.

Held-out designs remain outside study-specific training, tuning, and method
selection until evaluation. With an opaque pretraining corpus, this separation
reduces leakage from the current study but cannot prove that a model never
encountered the design. Randomly splitting rows is also weak when nearby rows
share a repository, generator, workload trace, or time period. A useful split
must expose the transfer the project cares about, such as a new design family,
workload, or later project revision [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage].

Successful designs can present a biased view of the space. When a project
retains the winning configuration while deleting failed synthesis runs,
unroutable netlists, and rejected alternatives, the remaining data cannot be
assumed to be an unbiased sample [@Rubin1976InferenceMissingData]. Retention
depends on outcome because failure itself affects whether a record survives.
The missing records are concentrated near the boundaries that later work most
needs to understand. A timing failure may report only that slack became
negative, and a crashed run may return no metric at all. Treating the surviving
results as though they were an unbiased sample makes the feasible region look
larger than it is.[^fn-censored-c04]

[^fn-censored-c04]: **Censored observation.** The result says that a value lies
beyond a threshold without measuring the value itself. A timing violation, for
example, may establish that a frequency target was not met without identifying
the highest frequency the design could sustain.

An execution history keeps those outcomes connected to the data rather than
discarding them after cleaning. It links each candidate to the prior state,
proposed change, conditions, tool return, run status, candidate status, and
design decision (@fig-execution-history). A completed run may be followed by
adoption, rejection, or an unresolved comparison. An infrastructure failure
supports none of those candidate outcomes and instead calls for repair or
rerun. Only an explicit decision to adopt a change creates a new design
version.

![**A versioned execution history separates run status, candidate outcome,
and design change.** A completed execution may be followed by adoption,
rejection, or an unresolved comparison. An infrastructure failure leads to
repair rather than a candidate verdict, and only explicit adoption creates a new design
state.](images/F5a-trajectory-record){#fig-execution-history width="85%"
fig-alt="Project history showing a valid result followed by an explicit
adoption and new state, a valid result that remains rejected or unresolved, and
an infrastructure failure that leads to repair while the design state remains
unchanged."}

The branches in @fig-execution-history are general history categories, not live
outcomes for the prospective Lighthouse cache study. An attempt that used stale
state would be an infrastructure failure. A valid 4\ MB result beyond a declared
physical limit could reject that candidate, while a completed 3\ MB comparison
could remain unresolved. The adoption branch lies outside this study, which may
recommend at most one candidate for later RTL evaluation but cannot create a
new design version. A prior result becomes a comparable sample only when its
declared-comparison status and recorded design, candidate, hardware, software,
workload, simulator, cache, power, SRAM, and PVT identifiers satisfy the
matching rule in @tbl-represented-problem. Other records can remain visible as
advisory context without becoming samples for this study.

Projects need negative records because successful designs are survivor
samples. Removing failed work makes both a dataset and an active study
optimistic near the feasibility boundary. The record should preserve why a run
failed without turning one local result into a universal prohibition
(@tbl-negative-traces).

| **Failed Run or Rejected Alternative** | **What to Keep** | **How Later Work Should Use It** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Synthesis or timing violation | Candidate, constraints, process assumptions, and failing paths. | Reconsider the candidate only after checking whether the relevant conditions still apply. |
| Unroutable or power-delivery failure | Netlist, placement conditions, density, congestion, or IR-drop result. | Identify the affected region and avoid treating the failure as a property of all similar designs. |
| Proxy improvement overturned later | Cheap estimate, later observation, and the conditions under which they diverged. | Reassess the proxy's useful scope before reuse. |
| Tool failure or crash | Command, inputs, environment identity, logs, and failure classification. | Repair the environment without recording the candidate as architecturally rejected. |
| Coverage gap | Missing workload, input, scenario, or architecture class. | Mark the boundary of the result rather than filling it with an assumption. |
| Reviewer rejection | Candidate, stated reason, risk, schedule, integration concern, and decision owner. | Preserve the rationale and revisit it only when the relevant conditions change. |
| Waiver or exception | Violated rule, justification, scope, owner, and expiration or review condition. | Prevent repeated work while keeping the exception visible. |

: **Rejected work remains useful when its conditions are recorded.** A later
architect can determine whether the same boundary still applies.
{#tbl-negative-traces tbl-colwidths="[27,34,29]"}

Each row pairs a failed result with the conditions and artifacts worth retaining
and the rule for later reuse. Timing, routing, or power-delivery failures may
constrain a candidate when the same design and conditions recur. A tool crash
instead returns to environment repair and must not become a candidate
rejection. Waivers similarly retain their scope, owner, and review condition
rather than turning an exception into a general pass.

The finished dataset records provenance, versions, access and licensing
conditions, acquisition cost, omitted populations, leakage risks, and the
reason each missing value is absent. These checks do not prove that the dataset
will support every later use. They make its support and omissions visible
enough for another architect to decide whether it applies.

## From Data to Project Knowledge

Recorded data, durable knowledge, and live state answer different questions.
Data consists of source artifacts, measurements, check results, and decisions
captured under stated conditions. Durable project knowledge includes
specifications, recurring design rationale, prior measurements, and resolved
decisions that may remain useful across tasks. Live project state names the
hardware, software, workload, constraints, unresolved issues, and accepted
revisions that apply now.

A method may need all three, but they change at different rates and come from
different responsible sources. A paper can explain why cache capacity may
affect misses, but it cannot override the checked-in design. A retrieved manual
can clarify a tool option, but it cannot establish which option the current run
used. An old run can reveal a risk, but it cannot automatically stand in for a
current measurement.

An architecture foundation model contributes broad prior knowledge learned
across sources. It can help retrieve a relevant mechanism, classify a familiar
interface pattern, or suggest which project document to inspect. It cannot
supply the current design revision, software image, workload, constraint, open
issue, or accepted tool result unless those facts arrive through current,
source-linked project context.

Knowledge also differs by where it lives (@tbl-knowledge-objects). Collapsing
all of these objects into the word *memory* or *context* hides their different
roles.

| **Object** | **What It Preserves** | **Responsible Source and Freshness Rule** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trained-model weights | Learned statistical regularities and general concepts. | Useful as prior knowledge, never the source of record for current project state. |
| Retrieval index and retrieved material | Source-linked manuals, papers, examples, and project documents selected for the current task. | The underlying source remains responsible. Version and date must match the use. |
| In-context working set | Instructions, selected sources, current state, and examples needed for one operation. | Transient assembly only. It does not become project state until a recorded update changes the responsible source. |
| Declared study | Question, comparator, scope, permitted changes, constraints, measurements, budget, and stopping conditions. | Remains the recorded definition of the comparison until the responsible owner records a revision. |
| Explicit design and software state | Current configuration, generated artifacts, software image, manifests, and linked constraints. | Current only when the designated sources agree and consistency checks pass. |
| Workload state | Trace, profile, population, phase definitions, sampling policy, and version. | Controls the workload condition only within its recorded coverage. |
| Project history | Prior candidates, tool runs, failures, decisions, and rationale linked to their conditions. | Records what happened then, but does not make that result applicable to the current version. |

: **Knowledge objects preserve different facts.** The current value comes from
the source responsible for that part of the project, not from whichever object
was supplied most recently.
{#tbl-knowledge-objects tbl-colwidths="[23,38,29]"}

There is no safe global rule that one file always wins. The declared study
defines the permitted comparison. The checked-in configuration and generated
artifact define implemented hardware state when they agree. The workload
manifest identifies the current trace. The specification states an interface
requirement. A review decision records whether a candidate advanced. When
responsible sources disagree, the project does not silently favor the most
convenient one. Work stops until the owner reconciles the mismatch or records a
revision.

Knowledge enters these objects on different schedules. General relationships
may be learned during model training. Manuals and prior reports may be
retrieved when needed. Current constraints belong in explicit project state,
not in model weights. Tool results append to project history only after their
identity and conditions are known. The durable update-path rule is simple
(@tbl-ingestion-timescales). Fast-changing facts need an explicit, versioned
path. Slow-changing knowledge can inform work but cannot override those facts.

| **Knowledge Path** | **Appropriate Content** | **Required Check Before Use** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model training or adaptation | General architecture concepts, recurring relationships, and interaction conventions. | Treat as prior knowledge and verify against responsible project sources. |
| Retrieval from a source collection | Manuals, specifications, prior studies, and versioned internal documents. | Confirm source identity, revision, and applicability. |
| Current working context | The subset of the declared study, state, history, and sources needed for the immediate task. | Confirm that it was assembled from current responsible sources. |
| Recorded project update | A revised comparison definition, design state, workload, constraint, decision, or accepted record. | Record owner, version, dependencies, and consistency checks. |

: **The update path should match how quickly a fact changes.** Current project
facts require explicit versioned updates. General knowledge remains advisory.
{#tbl-ingestion-timescales tbl-colwidths="[24,38,28]"}

Read the rows as different update paths rather than as increasing quality.
Model training and retrieval supply prior or source-linked material, and the
current working context assembles the subset needed for one operation. Only a
recorded project update changes the study definition, design, workload,
constraint, or accepted result. A fresh working context cannot turn advisory
knowledge into current project state.

Freshness is part of the distinction between durable knowledge and live state.
A current retrieval index can point to an old manual. A current design can be
paired with a trace captured from an earlier software image. A run directory
can contain a new report and an old configuration. Each file may look plausible
on its own while the combination describes no design that ever existed
(@fig-split-brain-causality).

![**A stale source can make a current design appear internally
consistent.** When a method reads an earlier specification or project state, it
can propose a change that violates the version now under
design.](images/F4b-split-brain-causality){#fig-split-brain-causality
width="100%" fig-alt="A stale reference state and a current project state lead
to an incompatible proposal. Version and freshness checks expose the mismatch
before the proposal reaches a costly tool flow."}

In the figure, the reference remains at V1 while the project advances to V2.
The proposal can therefore look consistent with the stale reference while
remaining incompatible with the design under development. The version mismatch
should stop that proposal before it reaches an expensive tool path.

The represented state can also drift from the artifact it claims to describe.
A parameter is renamed in the generator, a constraint is tightened directly in
an SDC file, or a block is replaced by hand. The state still says it is current,
but regenerating the design produces something different from the checked-in
artifact.

The direct check is to regenerate the artifact from the represented state and
compare the result with the repository. If the state cannot reproduce the
design it names, work that depends on it should not start. This check has a
clear limit. It works only where the state owns generation. A hand edit below
that level must be detected by another consistency check or made an explicit
part of state.

Source identity needs enough detail to support these checks. Depending on the
artifact, that may mean a version-control revision, content hash, tool and model
version, workload manifest, seed, process corner, timestamp, or named owner. The
representation should keep only what the study needs, but it cannot omit the
identity required to decide whether two records describe the same conditions.

Current state also has a maintenance cost. A freshness check reports a
condition at one moment. It does not keep the state current. Each source that
could change the decision needs a named owner and an invalidation trigger. A
new design revision, compiler release, workload capture, tool calibration,
constraint, library, process assumption, or expired waiver can make some part
of the represented problem stale.

When a trigger occurs, the owner determines which dependent artifacts and
results are affected. The response may be to regenerate an artifact, rerun a
consistency check, recapture data, recalibrate a model, repeat a measurement, or
mark the earlier result unavailable for the current comparison. The dependency
links matter because they keep a compiler update from forcing unrelated
physical work while ensuring that a changed cache generator reaches the
configurations, RTL, constraints, tests, and results that depend on it.

This maintenance consumes the same resources that data acquisition does.
Regeneration and checking use compute, licenses, storage, and tool time.
Recapturing a workload or recalibrating a model uses data and engineering time.
Broken links and source conflicts require diagnosis and review. Those recurring
costs should remain separate in the project record so that maintaining a rich
representation is not treated as free and so a later evaluation can see
whether the retained state repaid its cost.

Not every source should be maintained forever. When refresh cost exceeds the
value of keeping a source live, the project can narrow the representation,
freeze a versioned snapshot with an explicit review condition, or retain the
missing relationship as a blind spot. A source with no owner, invalidation
trigger, or affordable refresh path is historical context, not current project
state.

Current data and knowledge can now be translated into forms that learned and
conventional methods can use. The next distinction is between the native
artifact and the representations derived from it.

## From Architecture Artifacts to Learned Representations

A project can have the right facts and still represent them badly. The encoding
decides which designs can be expressed, which dependencies remain connected,
and which changes a later method will regard as nearby. These are architecture
consequences.

Raw text is useful for explanation but weak as the sole representation of a
design. It can describe an L2 change without identifying the configuration
field, affected interfaces, or companion constraints. Tool-facing
representations add structure. Parameter schemas enumerate legal values.
Abstract syntax trees and data-flow graphs preserve relationships that a token
sequence makes difficult to inspect. Typed intermediate representations can
reject malformed constructions before expensive execution. Parameterized
generators can expose a bounded set of changes while retaining the lowering
path to RTL.

Typed representations are not safe in general. They reject only violations
covered by their types and checks. SystemVerilog specifies logic, hierarchy,
interfaces, and verification constructs [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. FIRRTL and
typed dialects in Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) expose operations,
types, and compiler transformations [@CIRCT]. Companion formats such as
Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) and Unified Power Format (UPF) carry timing
and power intent [@SynopsysSDC; @IEEE2024UPF]. Each preserves different
properties (@tbl-representation-formats).

| **Representation** | **What It Makes Explicit** | **What Still Requires Attention** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SystemVerilog or VHDL | Logic, hierarchy, interfaces, and behavior in the HDL. | Width conventions, connectivity, unknown values, verification intent, and all properties not established by compilation. |
| Typed hardware IR such as FIRRTL or a CIRCT dialect | Operations, types, connectivity, and transformations supported by the IR. | Legal designs the IR cannot express, semantic correctness, lowering, verification, and physical realization. |
| Parameter schema and generator | Named mutable fields, legal values, and a reproducible path to generated artifacts. | Whether the generator and checked-in artifacts agree and whether dependent collateral changes with the design. |
| SDC, UPF, and other constraint collateral | Timing, power intent, domains, path references, and implementation assumptions. | Hierarchical-name coupling, stale paths, waived checks, and consistency with the RTL. |
| Graph or spatial representation | Connectivity, topology, adjacency, or physical location. | Features omitted from nodes and edges, write-back to tool inputs, and physical rules not encoded in the graph. |
| Learned embedding or latent feature vector | Statistical similarity and directions learned from the data supplied during training or adaptation. | Exact artifact identity, hierarchy, topology, order, units, legality, constraints, uncertainty, source coverage, and check results. |

: **A representation makes some properties explicit and leaves others for
later checks.** Choosing one also chooses which legal designs are easy,
difficult, or impossible to express.
{#tbl-representation-formats tbl-colwidths="[24,34,32]"}

HDL and typed IR expose logic, types, and connectivity while leaving semantic
correctness and physical feasibility for other checks. Schemas and generators
expose legal fields and lowering, while SDC and UPF expose timing and power
intent but remain coupled to names and current RTL. Graph and spatial forms
preserve only the topology, features, or locations they encode. A learned
vector exposes similarities useful to a later method but does not carry every
exact property of its source.

An embedding is a learned vector that places artifacts with similar modeled
features near one another. It can support retrieval, clustering, prediction,
generation, or adaptation [@BengioEtAl2013RepresentationLearning]. It is one
learned representation among several, not a compressed replacement for the
source artifact. The project must retain a link back to the exact source and to
the properties that cannot safely be recovered from learned similarity.

A learned representation also needs a task-specific fitness test. The project
states the learning objective and training data, names changes that should
leave the representation invariant, and names distinctions that must remain
visible. It then probes neighbors and counterexamples on held-out design
groups. If a representation drives artifact generation or mutation, proposed
changes must round-trip to the native representation and pass the applicable
legality and tool checks. An embedding that supports retrieval can still be
unfit for prediction or design modification when its geometry collapses a
topological, timing, or physical distinction needed by the later task.

Native sources can therefore feed several derived forms without surrendering
their original meaning. The useful question is which capability a derived form
enables and which exact information must remain linked outside it
(@tbl-source-representation-capability).

| **Native Source** | **Structured or Learned Representation** | **Capability It Can Support** | **Exact Information That Stays Linked** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Specification, manual, or design document | Versioned text chunks, typed requirement records, retrieval index, or text embedding. | Retrieve requirements, rationale, interface descriptions, and prior decisions. | Source identity, revision, access status, exact requirement text, and responsible owner. |
| Source code, RTL, netlist, or compiler IR | Token sequence, abstract syntax tree, typed IR, connectivity graph, or learned graph representation. | Inspect structure, propose bounded edits, retrieve similar blocks, or estimate a named property. | Native artifact, hierarchy, types, topology, legal transformations, companion constraints, and tool-check results. |
| Trace, performance counter stream, or profile | Phase record, sequence, time series, aggregate feature vector, or learned workload embedding. | Characterize phases, retrieve similar behavior, select samples, or predict a scoped response. | Input, software version, event order, timestamps, scale, sampling policy, units, and coverage. |
| Floorplan, physical database, or tool report | Geometry, spatial graph, typed report fields, image-like tensor, or learned physical representation. | Retrieve related layouts, localize physical pressure, or estimate a declared implementation property. | Coordinate system, units, design and tool version, mode, corner, constraints, waivers, uncertainty, raw artifact, and returned check status. |

: **Derived representations add capabilities only while exact architecture
facts stay connected to their sources.** Text, graphs, sequences, spatial
forms, and embeddings expose different properties, so the project retains the
native artifact and the conditions that make each derived view meaningful.
{#tbl-source-representation-capability tbl-colwidths="[20,28,24,28]"}

Read each row from the native source through a useful derived form to the
capability it supports. The last column is deliberately not another learned
feature list. It protects source identity, hierarchy, topology, order, units,
legality, exact constraints, uncertainty, and returned check results in forms
that another tool or architect can inspect.

::: {.callout-field-note title="The missing level shifter"}
A text-based proposal connects logic across two voltage domains without a level
shifter. The code passes syntax checks, but the represented design omitted the
power-domain relationship that made the connection illegal. This composite
example captures the real lesson. Better prose would not fix the problem. The
design state must carry the domains and the required crossing rule in a form
the tool path can check.
:::

Hardware is concurrent and relational. A netlist is a graph, a memory hierarchy
is a topology, and a floorplan adds spatial coordinates. Graph encodings can
preserve fan-in, fan-out, connectivity, and structural locality more directly
than a one-dimensional token stream. DeepGate2, for example, learns over
and-inverter graphs rather than treating a circuit only as text
[@ShiEtAl2023DeepGate2]. A graph still omits any property not attached to its
nodes, edges, or surrounding state. Logical adjacency is not physical
proximity, and a graph without placement cannot establish wire delay.

Mirhoseini and colleagues' macro-placement work provides a useful
representation example. The chip was represented with graph structure for
connectivity and a grid-like canvas for legal placement. Those choices exposed
relationships and spatial actions that flat RTL text did not
[@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement]. The result
does not establish that one placement method is generally best. It shows that a
method can search only after the architecture problem has been translated into
a form that preserves the relationships relevant to the task. The placement
method and its objective belong with optimization in
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization rather than in this chapter.

## Choosing and Connecting Representations

No single representation should carry every architecture responsibility. The
native artifact preserves exact content and remains the object that tools build
or check. Explicit structures expose hierarchy, topology, order, units,
constraints, and legal transformations. Retrieved context supplies
source-linked requirements and rationale. Learned representations can support
similarity, retrieval, prediction, generation, or adaptation, but they do not
replace those exact forms.

The representations must remain connected. A workload embedding without its
software and sampling record, a graph without its source hierarchy, or a report
vector without its units and tool conditions cannot be traced back to the fact
it is supposed to represent. The choice is therefore not one universal format.
It is a set of linked views chosen for the downstream capability and checked
against the properties each view must preserve.

### Permitted Changes and Invariants

A representation must separate what may change from what must remain fixed. In
the Lighthouse study, L2 capacity is the only mutable architecture field. The
2\ MB, 3\ MB, and 4\ MB choices must map to realizable cache configurations.
Cache policy, NoC topology, compiler, runtime, software image, workload, and the
rest of the memory system remain fixed. The 3\ W power envelope, 1.5\ mm^2^
macro-area limit, 2.5\ ns access-time allocation, and independent thermal and
IR-drop review remain required.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One permitted change, with its dependencies"}
**The declared move.** Select one realizable L2 capacity from 2\ MB, 3\ MB, and
4\ MB.

**What moves with it.** The capacity field, generated cache instance, and any
derived configuration needed to keep the artifact consistent.

**What does not move.** Cache policy, NoC topology, compiler, runtime, workload,
software image, memory system, and the declared limits and reviews.

**Why the boundary matters.** A proposal that changes capacity and compiler
behavior may be an interesting new study. It is not a valid candidate in this
comparison.
:::

The distinction also separates parametric and structural changes. A parametric
change selects a value within an existing structure, such as a legal cache
capacity or queue depth. A structural change alters the set of components or
relationships, such as adding a pipeline stage, replacing a mesh with a ring,
or inserting an accelerator. Structural changes require a different schema,
different dependent artifacts, and often a different study. Calling both
changes simply *edits* hides the difference.

System and software contracts matter even when they live outside the local
configuration. A new vector instruction affects the ISA, compiler, runtime,
and verification plan, and it may also require control and status register
changes. A memory organization that
improves average latency but violates the memory consistency model is not a
legal system design. Backward compatibility, interface standards, and
software assumptions must appear as dependencies or invariants rather than
remaining with the one experienced engineer who remembers them.

Physical collateral is coupled in the same way. Timing and power-intent files
often refer to exact hierarchical paths. Renaming or moving a block without
updating SDC or UPF can leave a constraint attached to the wrong design object
or to nothing [@Synopsys2025ConstraintMapping; @IEEE2024UPF]. A legal change
therefore includes its required companion changes. The representation should
make that group visible so a later method cannot improve one file while
silently invalidating another.

Fixed conditions may also be a set rather than one point. Multi-corner,
multi-mode analysis represents a physical design across operating modes and
process, voltage, and temperature corners [@Synopsys2025ConstraintMapping].
A candidate must retain the same identity across the declared condition matrix,
and each result must name the condition it covers. A typical-corner result
cannot silently stand in for a fast-corner hold check or a low-power operating
mode.

### Encoding Changes the Geometry

Even a correct list of legal values imposes a geometry on later search. Suppose
cache capacity is encoded on a linear numerical axis. A move from 512\ KB to
1\ MB then appears to be the same distance as a move from 4\ MB to 4.5\ MB.
The architectural effects are unlikely to be comparable, and 4.5\ MB may not
be realizable with the available SRAM macros. The encoding has created a
misleading neighborhood and an impossible point.

Two checks expose the problem. First, compare adjacent steps at different parts
of the encoded range. If equal encoded steps produce very different changes in
the architectural quantity of interest, the distance is misleading. Second,
ask whether every encoded point lowers to a configuration the tools can build.
An index over realizable macro organizations may be better than a continuous
capacity value. A logarithmic capacity axis may better reflect some cache
relationships than a linear one. These are design inferences for this example,
not prescriptions from one modeling paper. More broadly, classical
architecture design-space models use transformations and nonlinear terms when
parameter effects and interactions are not well represented on the original
axes [@LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling].

The lesson does not prescribe an optimizer. It precedes method selection.
Generation, prediction, and optimization all inherit the reachable set and
neighborhood created here. A poor encoding can make any of them waste effort
on impossible candidates or miss useful ones that were never expressible.

### Cross-Layer Relationships Need Provenance

Freshness also runs vertically through the stack. A high-level decision such as
adding a prefetcher may be lowered through generators, RTL, synthesis,
placement, and timing analysis. If a later timing failure cannot be connected
back to the architecture construct that produced it, the design state
fragments when the team most needs an explanation.

Cross-layer provenance records those relationships. It connects architecture
intent to the implementation objects and constraints that realize it. It does
not prove that every transformation preserved meaning. It makes the chain
inspectable and can localize a missing link or failed consistency check.
Detecting semantic loss still requires a check for the property that should
have survived.

Common architecture artifacts become reusable only when their hidden context is
made visible (@tbl-representation-debt).

| **Artifact** | **What It Preserves** | **What It Often Hides** | **Resulting Blind Spot** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Paper or plot | Reported claim, result, and comparison. | Tool flags, failed candidates, and tuning history. | The endpoint is visible but the path cannot be reconstructed. |
| Workload trace | Captured input behavior and measurements. | Population, coverage, version, sampling, and privacy filters. | The design may be optimized for an unrepresentative slice. |
| Simulator configuration | Model settings and selected options. | Defaults, unsupported states, calibration limits, and dependent software. | A number may be trusted outside the simulator's useful scope. |
| RTL or EDA report | Implementation-facing structure or feedback. | Process assumptions, constraints, waived warnings, and intent. | A locally valid artifact may not satisfy the system decision. |
| Cross-layer mapping | Links from architecture choices to lower-level objects. | Intermediate transformations not recorded in the mapping. | A physical failure may not be traceable to the choice that caused it. |
| Review note | Judgment, rationale, risk, and decision. | Unstated assumptions or alternatives never entered into the record. | Later work remembers the verdict but not its conditions. |
| Rejected candidate | A boundary and a negative result. | Failure reason, tool path, workload, or design version. | The team either repeats the failure or excludes too much. |

: **Architecture artifacts are reusable only within their recorded context.**
Provenance, assumptions, constraints, and coverage expose what each artifact
does and does not support.
{#tbl-representation-debt tbl-colwidths="[20,28,27,25]"}

Read across from an artifact's visible content through its hidden context to
the unsupported inference that can follow. A paper, plot, or review note may
preserve an endpoint or verdict without the path and conditions that produced
it. An RTL or EDA report may be locally valid without supporting the system
decision, while a cross-layer mapping can still hide an intermediate
transformation. Reuse therefore depends on preserving the context that rules
out each blind spot, not on the artifact type alone.

### Blind Spots and Known Unknowns Stay Visible

An adequate representation is not one that contains everything. It states what
it contains, what it omits, and the scope within which it remains useful.
Building a complete digital description of a modern system would cost more than
most studies could justify and would still miss something.

Blind spots are omitted or unobserved relationships that could matter. The
Lighthouse cache representation has no detailed floorplan or congestion result,
no completed thermal or IR-drop review, and no guarantee that
`XR-TRACE-A` covers every deployed workload condition. Known unknowns are
questions already recognized but not yet resolved, such as whether a larger
cache improves tail frame time enough to advance.

The distinction matters. A known unknown can be planned for. A blind spot may
surface only after a later tool, reviewer, or field observation exposes it.
Both should remain visible so that a later method does not convert missing
information into an assumed favorable value.

For this bounded study, @tbl-represented-problem provides the minimum useful
problem description. It contains enough identity and context to reconstruct
the comparison, expose
legal changes, and recognize when the representation is no longer useful. A
longer-lived or more consequential use needs more retained history and source
identity. The rules for claims that leave the project belong to the later
discussion of decision responsibility.

The chapter's distinctions now come together in one problem description.

| **Part of the Problem** | **Representation for the Lighthouse Cache Study** |
| --- | --- |
| Study identity and question | Illustrative study `XR-L2-CAP-A`, comparison definition revision `CONTRACT-A`, and current design revision `XR-COMPUTE-A`. The decision is which, if either, of the 3\ MB and 4\ MB candidates should advance to RTL evaluation against the rerun 2\ MB baseline. These identifiers instantiate the declared study in @sec-architecture-20-ontology. |
| Current hardware | Baseline artifact `L2-2M-A` is the checked-in 2\ MB design generated from revision `XR-COMPUTE-A`. The hardware owner is responsible for the configuration, generator revision, generated cache instance, and linked implementation collateral. |
| Verification dependencies | Each candidate retains the versioned reference behavior, testbench or properties, coverage intent, interface and reset assumptions, and required checks named by the declared study. The representation records these dependencies without claiming that they are adequate. |
| Fixed hardware and software state | Cache policy `CACHE-POLICY-A`, NoC `NOC-A`, memory-system configuration `MEMSYS-A`, 2\ GHz microarchitecture, compiler `COMPILER-A`, runtime `RUNTIME-A`, and RISC-V software image `SW-BASE-A`. Their responsible hardware or software owner controls each identifier. |
| Workload state | Workload snapshot `XR-TRACE-A`, including stable frame identifiers and boundaries, collection policy, and workload owner. |
| Candidate set and mapping | The field `l2.capacity` admits exactly `2MB`, `3MB`, and `4MB`, which lower to candidate artifacts `L2-2M-A`, `L2-3M-A`, and `L2-4M-A`. The 2\ MB artifact is the rerun baseline. |
| Permitted change | Only `l2.capacity` may change. Cache policy, associativity, NoC topology, compiler, runtime, memory system, and all other architecture choices remain fixed. |
| Constraints and required checks | This study checks modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power at or below 3\ W, cache macro area at or below 1.5\ mm^2^, and modeled access time at or below 2.5\ ns. Thermal and IR-drop reviews remain independent later requirements. |
| Relationships to preserve | Capacity may change miss behavior, which may change the frame-time distribution. It also changes macro organization and may change power, area, access time, and later physical integration. Workload, software, cache policy, and memory-system conditions must remain tied to every comparison. |
| Source identity | Comparison definition `CONTRACT-A`; design `XR-COMPUTE-A`; hardware, software, and workload identifiers above; cycle-level simulator `SIM-A`; cache model `CACHE-A`; power model `PM-A`; SRAM model `SRAM-A`; and process, voltage, and temperature assumptions `PVT-A`. The study record names the owner of each source. |
| History | The initial live history is empty. A prior result enters comparable history only when the declared study permits reuse and its design, candidate, hardware, software, workload, simulator, cache, power, SRAM, and PVT identities match. A nonmatching result may remain linked as advisory context but is not a sample for this study. Because the study in @sec-architecture-20-ontology is prospective, its definition and planned checks constrain the represented problem but create no entry in execution history. |
| Freshness checks | Recorded versions or hashes, named owners, timestamps where needed, and a successful regeneration or consistency check between represented state and the checked-in artifact. |
| Blind spots | No detailed floorplan or congestion result, no completed thermal or IR-drop review, incomplete workload coverage beyond `XR-TRACE-A`, and any hardware effect not modeled by the declared tools. |
| Known unknowns | Whether either larger cache improves 99th-percentile frame time enough to advance, and whether later physical review will uncover an effect absent from the current representation. |
| Study boundary | Four cycle-level executions including infrastructure reruns, one SRAM evaluation per capacity, and a decision to recommend at most one candidate for later RTL study. No implementation or product commitment is authorized. |
| Exclusions and useful scope | Cache-policy, prefetching, coherence, NoC, compiler, software-scheduling, floorplanning, thermal-signoff, IR-drop-signoff, security, reliability, and product-cost changes are excluded. The representation supports only the declared cache-capacity comparison, not a complete model of the XR subsystem or product. |

: **The represented problem makes the declared study inspectable.** It connects
the current design, workload, legal changes, verification dependencies,
history, freshness, and limits without selecting a method or claiming a
result.
{#tbl-represented-problem tbl-colwidths="[24,66]"}

Read the upper rows as identity and current state, the middle rows as the legal
change and relationships it must preserve, and the lower rows as provenance,
freshness, limits, and useful scope. The decisive link connects candidate
mapping to constraints. `l2.capacity` changes one generated cache artifact
while the workload, software, cache policy, and memory system remain tied to
every comparison. The blind-spot, boundary, and exclusion rows explain why this
representation cannot support implementation or product commitment.

The fields may live in several project systems. What matters is that every
artifact refers to the same study, design version, workload version, and
candidate. A directory full of individually valid files is not a represented
problem if no one can tell which files describe the same comparison.

### Inputs to Method Choice

@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization needs an inspectable problem,
not a prescribed technique. The Lighthouse problem description therefore
passes forward the source-linked state developed throughout the chapter.
@tbl-represented-problem summarizes the worked Lighthouse problem, while the
earlier sections supply its sample conditions and acquisition cost, checked
data and failures, connected native and learned representations, and the blind
spots and freshness limits that bound their use.

It intentionally contains no proposed next candidate, predicted consequence,
surrogate, optimizer, acceptance threshold for a model, or execution result.
Those additions would answer questions this chapter has not yet asked.
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization can now decide whether the
work should proceed directly to tools or add a method. If an added method is
justified, the study first names the engineering job, then chooses a method
family (generation, prediction, or optimization) or a justified combination,
together with a conventional, learned, or hybrid implementation.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces can decide how the chosen work
is connected to tools. @sec-feedback-verification-trust can decide what
feedback means. The order protects the study from being reshaped around the
first available method.

The handoff is inadequate if it cannot reproduce or identify the current
design, if it hides a controlling hardware-software or physical relationship,
if its legal actions bundle undeclared changes, if its sources disagree without
a resolution, or if no one can state where the representation is useful.

## Open Research Questions

The open problems concern collecting costly and incomplete architecture data,
preserving design meaning across learned and explicit forms, and keeping
project knowledge current.

### Building Architecture Datasets

**How should an AI-assisted study allocate a limited data-acquisition budget
across tools with different costs and coverage?** More samples from a cheap
source may leave the property that controls the decision unobserved, while a
few expensive samples may cover too little of the design and workload space.

**How can AI-assisted methods learn from failed and censored design data without
treating every local failure as a universal boundary?** Failed runs contain
valuable information near feasibility limits, but their meaning depends on the
exact design, tools, workload, and constraints that produced them.

**How can dataset construction expose a coverage hole that no current source
has named?** Declared omissions can be recorded directly, but unrecognized
missing relationships may appear only after a later tool, reviewer, or workload
exposes them.

### Preserving Relationships Across Representations

**Which representation lets a method preserve the neighborhood that matters
for a given architecture decision?** A scalar schema, graph, spatial model, or
typed IR makes different relationships visible and creates different notions
of adjacency. The wrong neighborhood can admit illegal candidates or hide
feasible ones, while the relevant notion changes with the decision.

**How can a learned representation support similarity without hiding exact
architecture constraints?** Identity, hierarchy, topology, order, units,
legality, uncertainty, and check results may not survive in one learned vector.

**How should a method represent hardware and software dependencies when no
single artifact owns the interface between them?** ISA, compiler, runtime,
firmware, and microarchitecture changes often cross repositories and
organizational boundaries. An apparently local change can therefore invalidate
assumptions that no single tool or team sees.

### Keeping Project State Useful

**How can an automated method detect that represented state no longer describes
the artifact it names?** Regeneration catches divergence where state owns the
build, but hand edits, generated collateral, and external tool transformations
create additional paths for drift.

**What is the smallest current project record that can correct a foundation
model's broad prior?** Too little state makes a result uninterpretable, while
indiscriminate capture creates cost, privacy, and maintenance burdens that can
outlive the study.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Preserve exact facts before learning from them"}
Architecture data remains useful only when its source, design and workload
identity, units, conditions, cost, and limits survive dataset construction and
representation. A learned representation may add capability, but it does not
replace the native artifact or current project state that later checks must
inspect.
:::

Architecture data is not a collection of interchangeable labeled examples.
Specifications, code, RTL, traces, formal results, tool reports, rejected work,
and reviews carry different information. Workloads determine which behavior is
exercised, and every stored result remains tied to the design, software, tool,
conditions, and acquisition cost that produced it. Coverage matters more than
row count.

A usable dataset makes those dependencies inspectable. It aligns source
identities and units, checks versions and lineage, preserves failures and
censored results, separates tool problems from measured design violations, and
documents held-out designs, access limits, omissions, and leakage risks. This
work turns heterogeneous sources into data that a later method can use without
making unsupported comparisons look clean.

Data does not replace project knowledge or live state. A foundation model can
supply broad prior knowledge, and retrieval can bring source-linked material
into the current task. The checked-in design, software image, workload,
constraints, unresolved issues, and accepted results still come from current
project sources. A state that cannot identify or reproduce the artifact it
names is not current.

Native artifacts, typed structures, graphs, sequences, spatial forms, retrieved
text, and learned representations each expose different properties. Embeddings
can support useful similarity and adaptation, but identity, hierarchy,
topology, order, legality, units, exact constraints, uncertainty, and returned
check results remain linked outside them. The architect chooses connected
representations that preserve the relationships controlling the current
question and expose what remains missing.

The chapter's output is the represented problem in
@tbl-represented-problem. It contains source identity, workload, sample
conditions and cost, checked data, current state, legal changes, dependencies,
history, linked representations, freshness, blind spots, and known unknowns for
the Lighthouse cache study. It does not determine how to explore that problem.
That source-linked description gives method choice a firm starting point.
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization can decide whether to proceed
directly to tools or add prediction, generation, optimization, or a
conventional or hybrid combination without inventing missing state.
